analysis.one_liner: Requires companies and agencies to secure personal data and tell people when a breach puts them at risk.
analysis.headline: The bill cleared the Senate Judiciary Committee on October 20, 2005 and was placed on the Senate calendar, but the Senate never voted on it before that Congress ended in January 2007.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have set the first national rules for data security: any company or government agency holding sensitive personal information would have to keep reasonable safeguards and tell people when a breach creates a significant risk of identity theft. But the same bill would have overridden stronger state breach-notification laws, barred consumers from suing, and capped federal fines at $250,000 per breach no matter how many people were affected. It cleared committee but never came up for a Senate vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers who would get a guaranteed right to notice when their Social Security number, driver's license number, or financial account details are exposed in a breach, including residents of states that had no breach law of their own. Companies holding data would also benefit from one uniform federal standard instead of a patchwork of state rules, capped fines, and the elimination of class actions.

how_it_helps.text: Any agency or company that owns or licenses computerized data containing sensitive personal information must implement and maintain reasonable security and notification procedures to protect it from unauthorized access, use, or disclosure.

An entity that suffers a breach posing a significant risk of identity theft must notify every U.S. resident whose sensitive information was compromised, without unreasonable delay, with a clear notice describing the breach and a toll-free number or website for help.
State attorneys general are authorized to sue on behalf of their residents to enforce the law and obtain restitution or compensation up to the bill's monetary limits.

analysis.who_pays: Companies, financial institutions, insurers, and government agencies holding consumer data would bear the cost of security upgrades and breach notifications, plus fines of up to $250,000 per breach for failing to notify. Consumers would pay in weaker protections: their right to sue would be eliminated, and stricter state laws would be wiped out by the federal floor.
analysis.who_pays_short: Data-holding companies; consumers lose state protections

drawbacks.text: The company itself decides, after its own 'reasonable investigation,' whether a breach poses a significant risk of identity theft — so the entity responsible for the breach is the one that decides whether victims get told.
The bill states that no private right of action or class action may be brought under it, cutting off the main legal tool consumers had for holding firms accountable after a breach.
Fines are capped at $250,000 per breach, no matter how many millions of people were affected.

Section 5 would supersede any state law 'that relates in any way' to information security or breach notification, wiping out stronger state standards — including states that required notice without a 'significant risk' showing.
A safe harbor says a company with its own notification policy is in compliance if it simply follows its own policy after a breach.

A state attorney general cannot recover damages for residents until the company has first been enjoined and then violated that injunction, and the U.S. Attorney General or the industry's own 'functional regulator' can step in and block the state's action.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For consumers in states with no breach law, a national right to notice was a real gain — California's 2002-style notification laws were spreading, but most states had none in 2005. For consumers in states with stronger laws, the bill was a net loss: it replaced tougher state standards with a federal rule that let the breaching company decide whether notice was needed, capped penalties, and barred class actions. On balance it traded strong, uneven state protections for a weaker, uniform federal floor.

outcome.mechanism: The Judiciary Committee approved it and put it on the Senate's calendar in October 2005, but the Senate never took it up for a vote before that Congress ended in January 2007.

narrative.text: Senator Jeff Sessions introduced the bill on June 28, 2005, and it was referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee.
On October 20, 2005, the Judiciary Committee ordered the bill reported favorably without amendment, and Chairman Arlen Specter reported it to the Senate.
The bill was placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders (Calendar No. 252) on October 20, 2005 — a waiting position for floor action that never came.
No further action was taken before the 109th Congress ended on January 3, 2007.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Companies holding consumer data came out ahead: the bill never became law, so no company faced its capped fines or had to adopt its notification rules — and firms also avoided the federal preemption fight, since the stronger state breach laws that had already passed stayed on the books while most states remained without any law.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Data-holding companies that avoided new rules

sides.party_line_note: Only Republicans are on record in support — sponsor Sessions and one Republican cosponsor — and no floor vote ever occurred, so the chamber's full partisan split on the bill is unknown.

industries.industry: Companies holding consumer data (retailers, data brokers, and general business)
industries.note: The bill imposed new security and notification duties on them, but in exchange gave them a uniform federal standard, a $250,000 fine cap, no class actions, and override of stricter state laws. Because the bill let the breaching company itself decide whether victims got notice, its liability protections ran against consumers' interest in being told.

industries.industry: Banks, credit unions, and other financial institutions
industries.note: Financial firms would face the same notification rules, but compliance would be enforced by their own sector regulators (the bill's 'functional regulators' like the OCC, Fed, and FDIC) rather than a general consumer-protection agency — a familiar and industry-friendly enforcement arrangement. Preemption of stricter state financial-privacy and notification rules also worked in their favor.

Before notifying more than 1,000 people of a breach, a company must coordinate with the nationwide credit bureaus and shape its notice around them, making the bureaus the mandatory channel through which breach victims learn their responsibilities under the Fair Credit Reporting Act. Every large breach would push affected consumers toward the credit bureaus' fraud-alert and monitoring systems.

Insurers would be overseen by state insurance authorities and brokers and investment advisers by the SEC as their enforcement regulators. They gained the same liability limits and preemption as other covered firms while facing new notification obligations.
